OWASP's SSRF cheat sheet gives user-supplied image URLs and webhooks as typical entry points; a document renderer that loads remote images is the same pattern.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Egress filtering, isolation and detecting SSRF
question: Why is an alert on VPC Flow Logs records for 169.254.169.254 not a working detection for metadata SSRF on AWS?
options: Flow logs are encrypted
AWS documents that flow logs do not record traffic to and from the instance metadata address at all
Flow logs only exist for IPv6
The metadata service uses UDP
explain: Metadata traffic never appears in flow logs, so an alert on it can never fire. Use the IMDS CloudWatch metrics, host-level monitoring and credential-use signals (CloudTrail, GuardDuty) instead.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Log4Shell response: versions, mitigations and detection
question: A server running a vulnerable Log4j sits behind a firewall that denies all outbound connections except to its database. An attacker sends the lookup string. What is the most likely result?
options: Full remote code execution as usual
The lookup triggers an outbound connection attempt that the firewall denies, so the chain breaks and the denied connection shows up in firewall logs
The database is compromised instead
Nothing at all is logged anywhere
explain: The classic chain needs an outbound connection to the attacker's directory server. Default-deny egress breaks it and produces a denial log entry, which is excellent evidence. Patch anyway: lookups that read local data, such as environment variables, can still leak them into logs.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: When front end and back end disagree: smuggling and ProxyLogon
question: In ProxyLogon, why did the back end perform privileged actions for an unauthenticated attacker?
options: The attacker cracked an admin password
Exchange had no back end
The front end forwarded the attacker-routed request using the Exchange server's own Kerberos identity, which the back end trusted
The attacker used request smuggling
explain: The front end lent its own credentials to a request whose destination the attacker chose: SSRF with a confused deputy. The fix validated the routing value as a host name and stopped the front end from authenticating such requests as itself.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop
question: Why can't the scheduler simply build batch k+1 while batch k runs, with no extra machinery?
options: Batch k+1 needs batch k's sampled tokens as its inputs, which are not known until batch k finishes; SGLang uses future-token placeholders resolved on the GPU
The GPU cannot run two kernels in a row
Python cannot start a second thread
The radix tree must be rebuilt from scratch every step
explain: For decoding, each step's input is the previous step's output. Overlap therefore needs a way to refer to tokens that do not exist yet. The release notes describe resolving this dependency with future tokens and careful CUDA event synchronization.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: A*: steering the search with a lower bound
question: To speed things up, someone divides straight-line km by 30 km/h instead of the network's top speed of 60 km/h. What is the risk?
options: None; any distance-based estimate keeps A* optimal
A* will settle more nodes than before
The heuristic may now overestimate on fast roads, so A* can return a slower route than the optimum
The algorithm may loop forever
explain: At 30 km/h each kilometer is estimated at 2 minutes, but a 60 km/h road covers it in 1. Overestimating breaks Theorem 1's condition, so optimality is no longer guaranteed. The survey notes such aggressive bounds speed things up only by giving up correctness.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: Frequency bins, resolution and spectral leakage
question: You record 2 s of data at 1000 Hz and need to tell apart tones at 50.0 Hz and 50.3 Hz. What helps?
options: Zero-pad to 8 times the length before the FFT
Sample at 4000 Hz instead of 1000 Hz for the same 2 s
Record for longer: at least several seconds, since the bin spacing is 1/duration
Apply a Hann window, which sharpens peaks
explain: Resolution is fs/N = 1/duration. Two seconds gives 0.5 Hz bins, too coarse for a 0.3 Hz gap; you need more than 1/0.3 = 3.3 s, and more still with a window, which widens peaks. A higher fs adds bins at high frequencies but keeps the spacing at 1/duration. Zero-padding only interpolates the same blurred spectrum.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Writing a vector loop: intrinsics, reductions and tails
question: You remove the scalar tail loop from sum_avx2 to save code. What happens for n = 19?
options: Nothing, the vector loop reads all 19 elements
It returns 136, silently dropping a[16], a[17] and a[18]
It crashes because the last load is out of bounds
It returns 190 but more slowly
explain: The vector loop stops at i = 16 because 16 + 8 > 19, so it never reads past the end. Without the tail the last 3 elements are never added: you get 136 instead of 190. Silent wrong answers like this are the classic SIMD bug.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
question: You ship a desktop app built with `-march=x86-64-v4` because benchmarks on your AVX-512 workstation looked great. Users with AVX2-only laptops report crashes at startup. What is the right fix?
options: Add -O3
Build for the baseline or x86-64-v3 and use target_clones or runtime checks for the AVX-512 hot loops
Switch to -ffast-math
Catch SIGILL and retry
explain: x86-64-v4 lets the compiler place AVX-512 instructions anywhere, including startup code. Build the bulk for a level every user has, and multiversion only the hot kernels so each CPU picks its best copy.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: The slab allocator: caches of ready-made objects
question: A slab holds 31 objects of 128 bytes in a 4096-byte page, with 32 bytes of in-page metadata. Without coloring, every slab's objects start at offset 0. What does coloring change?
options: It fits a 32nd object into the page by moving the metadata elsewhere
It uses the 96 leftover bytes to start each new slab's objects at a different offset, so hot fields of objects in different slabs map to different cache sets
It rounds the objects up to 256 bytes so each one is cache-line aligned
It marks freed objects with a pattern so use-after-free is detected
explain: 31 x 128 = 3968 bytes, plus 32 metadata leaves 96 spare bytes. Coloring spends that otherwise wasted space on an offset that varies per slab. (Filling freed memory with 0xdeadbeef is a separate debugging feature.)

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Moving weights from Megatron into SGLang
question: You move a working colocated job to separate pools and add `--update-weight-mode delta` but keep the default transport. What happens?
options: It fails at startup: delta mode requires `--update-weight-transport disk`
It runs, shipping deltas over NCCL
It silently falls back to full NCCL sync
It uses CUDA IPC because the engines are on the same nodes
explain: Argument validation rejects it at startup, and `create_weight_updater` asserts the same: delta mode needs disk transport and no colocation. Delta sync works by publishing versioned checkpoint directories that engines pull, not by broadcasting.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Train-rollout mismatch in slime: TIS, IcePop, R3 and score centering
question: An FP8-rollout run on an MoE model shows `tis_clipfrac` climbing from 0.002 to 0.1 over a few hundred rollouts while reward stalls. Following slime's guidance, which change comes first?
options: Raise --tis-clip to 20 so fewer tokens are clipped
Switch to --use-rollout-logprobs to skip the trainer recompute
Enable --use-rollout-routing-replay to remove routing flips at the source, keep TIS, and compare clipfrac and log-prob gap with that single change
Turn TIS off, since clipping shows it is not working
explain: On an MoE model a large share of the gap comes from expert selection, which R3 removes; it is independent of TIS. Widening the clip only lets outliers through, bypassing the recompute removes the correction (slime even refuses it with `--use-tis` under the PPO loss), and turning TIS off leaves the gap uncorrected. Change one mechanism at a time and watch the metrics.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Consensus under attack: Sybil, 51 percent and eclipse attacks
question: Why does proof of stake resist Sybil attacks even though creating validator identities is free?
options: Each identity must pass a know-your-customer check
Validators are chosen by IP address
Proof of stake uses longer hashes
Voting weight comes from staked ETH, so a thousand identities with no stake have no weight
explain: Weight follows the scarce resource, not the count of identities. Splitting 32 ETH into many identities does not add votes, and misbehaviour costs stake through slashing.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Access control and unprotected initializers: Parity 2017
question: The patched Parity check was `if (m_numOwners > 0) throw;`. Why did it not protect the library contract itself?
options: The modifier was missing from the library's code
The check read the library's own storage, where no owners had ever been set
Libraries cannot hold storage
selfdestruct bypasses all modifiers
explain: Through a wallet, the check reads the wallet's storage (owners set). Called directly, it reads the library's storage, which was never initialized, so the check passed.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: Front-running, MEV and commit-reveal
question: A swap is submitted with minimum output 0 and no deadline. What does that enable?
options: Nothing, minimum output 0 is the safest setting
A sandwich can fill it at any price, however bad
Reentrancy
Signature replay
explain: With no minimum, the trade accepts whatever price the front-running transaction creates. A realistic minimum output makes manipulated execution revert.

courseTitle: Smart contract and blockchain security
lessonTitle: When the fix or the compiler is the bug: Euler and Curve, 2023
question: Euler's donateToReserves was audited and fixed a real bug. What kind of test would most likely have caught the new flaw?
options: A gas benchmark
An invariant test that no sequence of a user's own actions makes their position profitably liquidatable
A test that the function emits an event
A front-end test
explain: The bug was a missing health check on one path. An invariant over all actions, run by a fuzzer, explores paths a reviewer of the diff did not consider.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: The alert lifecycle, and why the queue is not first come, first served
question: An analyst tries to close a case with the note "looks fine" and no verdict. Why should the case tool refuse?
options: Because closed cases cannot be reopened
Because without a verdict and a reason, nobody can review the decision or tune the rule, and real attacks dismissed this way are never found
Because every alert must be escalated to Tier 2 before closing
Because notes must be at least 100 characters
explain: The verdict and the evidence-based reason are what quality review and rule tuning run on. "Looks fine" cannot be checked by anyone, which is exactly how alerts get "dismissed without good reason".

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: When the attacker calls the help desk: MFA resets and new devices
question: A help desk resets MFA for a finance clerk at 10:00 after a call. At 10:05 the clerk's account signs in from a new device through an anonymising proxy and creates a mail rule forwarding all mail with "invoice" to an outside address. What do you do first?
options: Close: the help desk ticket shows the reset was authorised
Email the clerk to ask whether they set up the rule
Revoke the sessions and the new factor, remove the forwarding rule, and verify with the clerk by phone on the HR-listed number
Wait for a second alert to confirm
explain: The ticket proves only that someone called. A new device through a proxy within minutes, followed by a forwarding rule aimed at invoices, is classic account takeover. Contain first, then verify out of band. Emailing the account the attacker may control is the wrong channel.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Ransomware precursors, and deciding fast: Colonial Pipeline
question: Colonial shut down the whole pipeline although the ransomware was found on the IT network, not on the systems controlling the pipeline. According to the CEO's testimony, why?
options: Because they did not know where the attack started or how far it had spread, and stopping the pipeline was the surest way to keep it from reaching the OT network
Because the OT network had already been encrypted
Because the ransom note demanded it
Because regulators ordered the shutdown
explain: The testimony says the stop work order aimed to keep the malware from spreading to the OT network "if it had not already", because the origin and scope were unknown. It is a textbook decision under uncertainty, made by people with authority to make it.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: SOAR playbooks: what to automate and what to keep human
question: A playbook automatically blocks at the firewall every source IP that triggers a brute-force alert. What is the main risk?
options: Attackers, or simple misconfigurations, can make it block addresses you depend on, such as shared carrier IPs or partners, turning your own automation into a denial of service
Firewalls cannot block IPs automatically
It makes the SOC too fast
Brute-force alerts are always false positives
explain: The trigger is driven by input others control, and IPs are shared (lesson 5). Bound the action: never-block lists, expiry times, approval for anything that is not clearly hostile and clearly yours to block.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Warnings people heed: browser warnings and opinionated design
question: Which change would most reliably stop users proceeding to an attacker's site on a bank's domain with a forged certificate?
options: A longer warning text that explains certificates
A warning with a red background
The bank sends HSTS, so the browser refuses the connection with no option to proceed
Training customers to read certificate details
explain: HSTS removes the decision: for a known HSTS host the browser must terminate on any certificate error. Explanations and colours help adherence but still leave a click-through path.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: The help desk as an attack surface: MGM, Okta's warning and Clorox
question: Okta's 2023 report described callers asking help desks to reset all MFA factors for Super Administrators. Why target those accounts specifically?
options: They have weaker passwords
Admin accounts can change the identity system itself, opening every other account and application
Help desks cannot see who is an administrator
Super Administrators never use MFA
explain: Control of the identity provider's admin role let the attackers add their own identity provider and sign in as other users. One reset on the right account is worth hundreds on ordinary ones.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: What a lock really does: pin tumblers, master keys and key control
question: A contractor who held a grand master key leaves and does not return it. What does PE-3 call for?
options: Nothing, if the contractor signed a non-disclosure agreement
Change the locks the key opens, because a lost key remains valid until the cylinders are re-keyed
Disable the contractor's network account only
Install CCTV at the main entrance
explain: A mechanical key cannot be revoked remotely. Until the cylinders it opens are re-keyed, whoever holds it can use it, and copies may exist. PE-3 asks for changes when keys are lost or holders leave.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Testing the people layer: rules of engagement, ethics and metrics
question: Which pretext should an HR and legal review reject for a staff phishing test?
options: A fake shared-document notification from a colleague
A fake delivery notice
A fake invitation to an internal training session
A fake announcement of a holiday bonus during a period of financial hardship
explain: Lures that exploit real hopes or distress spend trust the security team needs, as GoDaddy's 2020 apology shows. The others are realistic without promising money or benefits people need.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Enforcing sparsity: L1, TopK and JumpReLU
question: You switch an SAE from L1 to TopK and keep everything else the same. Which hyperparameter replaces lambda as the main sparsity knob?
options: k, the number of latents kept per token
The learning rate
The number of latents M
The kernel bandwidth epsilon
explain: TopK sets sparsity directly: L0 equals k. There is no sparsity term in the loss, so there is no lambda to tune. Epsilon belongs to JumpReLU training.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
question: Why does the Scaling Monosemanticity steering recipe keep the SAE error term instead of feeding the edited reconstruction alone into later layers?
options: To make the latent's activation non-negative
Because the error term is always zero for TopK SAEs
So the only change to the activation is the chosen feature; dropping the error would also remove everything the SAE fails to reconstruct
To reduce memory use
explain: Replacing x with the reconstruction alone would apply two edits at once: the feature clamp and the loss of all unexplained structure. Keeping the error makes x' = x + (c - f_i) d_i.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance
question: Your fitted variogram has a large nugget, almost equal to the sill. What does this say about your sensors?
options: Readings are strongly correlated at all distances, so interpolation will be very accurate
The range must be zero, so kriging cannot be run
Even very close sensors disagree about as much as distant ones, so spatial interpolation adds little over the mean
Close sensors always agree exactly
explain: The nugget is the semivariance as distance approaches zero. If it is almost the sill, nearby pairs differ about as much as unrelated pairs: the measurable spatial structure is weak (or dominated by measurement error), and kriging estimates approach the mean.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Why decoding is slow and why checking guesses is cheap
question: Which claim about speculative decoding is correct?
options: It speeds up decoding by letting a smaller model answer the easy prompts
It trades a small amount of quality for latency, like quantization
It produces the same output distribution as the target model and only changes how many target passes are needed
It only works with greedy decoding
explain: Both original papers prove the sampled tokens follow the target's distribution for any draft. Quality is unchanged; speed depends on how well the draft guesses. Lesson 3 covers sampling, not just greedy.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Build it: speculative sampling with two real models
question: Your measured alpha is 0.85 and c is 0.47, so the formula predicts about 1.3x, but you measure 0.76x. Which measurement most likely explains the gap?
options: The time of one target pass over gamma + 1 positions compared with a one-token step
The TV distance between the output and p
The vocabulary size of the tokenizer
The per-position acceptance rate at position 1
explain: The formula assumes a verify pass costs one plain step. On this CPU it cost 2.3 to 2.7 steps in quiet runs; putting that into the denominator predicts 0.80x to 0.88x at gamma = 4, far closer to the measured 0.76x. Acceptance and TV distance were already accounted for.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Self-speculation: MTP heads, layer skipping and lookahead
question: Which method changes the weights of the backbone you end up serving?
options: Draft & Verify, because it skips layers
LayerSkip, whose layer dropout and early exit loss retrain the model, much like Medusa-2's fine-tuning
Lookahead decoding, because it updates the n-gram pool
Prompt lookup decoding
explain: Draft & Verify only skips layers at inference time, and lookahead and prompt lookup change no weights. LayerSkip trains (or continues pretraining) the model itself, so outputs are exact with respect to the retrained model, not the original one.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Word error rate: alignments, normalization and fair comparisons
question: A reference has 10 words. The aligned hypothesis has 2 substitutions, 1 deletion and 3 insertions. What is the WER?
explain: WER = (S + D + I) / N = (2 + 1 + 3) / 10 = 60%. Dividing by the hypothesis length (12 words) would give 50%, a common bug. 30% forgets the insertions.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Beyond the basic chunk: size classes, thread caches and fragmentation
question: After a traffic spike, a service using a size-class allocator frees 90 percent of its small objects, yet its resident memory barely drops. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The allocator must be leaking the freed objects
The kernel ignores munmap while the process is busy
Freed objects sit in caches, and most spans still hold a few live objects, so whole spans cannot be returned
Freed memory is zeroed, which keeps it resident
explain: A span or slab goes back to the page heap only when every object in it is free. Survivors scattered across many spans pin them all, and per-thread or per-CPU caches hold more. That is fragmentation, not a leak: the memory is reusable by the same process. Purging caches, malloc_trim with glibc, or a different allocator can help.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: When RAM runs out: page cache, file mappings, swap and thrashing
question: A box with no swap is under memory pressure. Which pages can the kernel reclaim?
options: Anonymous heap pages, by zeroing them
Only kernel data structures
Nothing until the OOM killer runs
Clean file pages by dropping them, and dirty file pages after writing them back
explain: File pages have a home on disk, so they can always be dropped (after write-back if dirty) and re-read later. Anonymous pages have no home except swap; with no swap they stay put, and if file pages are not enough the OOM killer is the last resort.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Directional ablation: what erasing the refusal direction reveals
question: You ablate a direction found as the harmful minus harmless mean difference at layer 12, at every layer. A fresh linear probe trained at layer 20 still separates harmful from harmless prompts. What does this show?
options: Nothing contradictory: the guarantee only covers the activations whose class means defined the direction; at layer 20 the means can differ along other directions
The ablation code must be broken, because ablation makes every concept unreadable at every layer
Linear probes always succeed, whatever edit is applied
LEACE would have made the concept unreadable at every layer at once
explain: Equal class means, and so linear guardedness, holds for the activations the mean difference was computed on. Later layers recompute features from everything else in the stream, and their class means can differ along new directions. LEACE has the same scope; concept scrubbing fits a separate eraser at each layer in turn.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Beyond one fixed vector: conditional, learned and monitoring uses
question: Persona-vector preventative steering adds the evil direction during fine-tuning on a dataset that induces evil. Why does this reduce evil in the final model?
options: The added vector cancels the training loss entirely
It makes the training data less evil
It removes the evil direction from the weights by orthogonalization
The steering already supplies the push toward the trait, so gradient descent has less reason to move the weights along that direction; the vector is removed at deployment
explain: Fitting the data requires movement along the persona direction. When the steering vector provides it during training, the weights need not change along it, and once the vector is switched off for deployment the trait expression stays low. It does not edit the data or orthogonalize weights.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Online filtering: EMA as a low-pass, Welford for anomaly flags
question: Two parallel tasks each computed Welford state for half of a sensor's readings. Can you get the exact overall variance?
options: No, variance needs all raw values in one place
Yes, by averaging the two variances
Yes, by combining (n, mean, M2) of both halves with a pairwise merge formula
Only if both halves have the same mean
explain: Averaging variances ignores the difference between the two means. Chan, Golub and LeVeque give a merge: M2 = M2a + M2b + delta squared x na x nb / (na + nb), with delta the difference of means. This is what makes mean and variance easy to parallelize across partitions.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Causal masks, teacher forcing and cross-attention
question: In encoder-decoder (cross) attention, where do the queries, keys and values come from?
options: Queries, keys and values all come from the encoder output
Queries from the encoder; keys and values from the decoder
Queries from the decoder; keys and values from the encoder output
Queries and keys from the decoder; values from the encoder
explain: The decoder is asking questions about the source, so it supplies the queries. The encoder output supplies the keys (what each source position offers) and the values (what gets copied). This lets every decoder position attend over all input positions.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: One layer end to end, in numbers and in code, and how it decodes
question: A position's sum x + Sublayer(x) is (2, 4, 6). What does LayerNorm output with gain 1, bias 0 and a negligible epsilon?
options: (2, 4, 6) divided by its length: about (0.27, 0.53, 0.80)
(-2, 0, 2), the vector minus its mean
About (-1.22, 0, 1.22): subtract the mean 4, divide by the standard deviation 1.63
(0, 0.5, 1), rescaled to the range 0 to 1
explain: The mean is 4 and the variance is (4 + 0 + 4)/3 = 8/3, so the standard deviation is 1.63. (2 - 4)/1.63 = -1.22, and so on. LayerNorm centers and scales by the standard deviation; dividing by the length is a different normalization, and subtracting the mean alone leaves the scale untouched.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Term-frequency saturation: what k1 controls
question: A product search team sees titles like "usb cable usb-c usb charger usb" outranking clean titles for the query usb. Which change to k1 most directly reduces the benefit of repeating a word?
options: Increase k1 from 1.2 to 5
Set b to 0
Decrease k1 from 1.2 to about 0.5
Leave k1, since BM25 already ignores repeats
explain: Lower k1 makes the factor saturate sooner, so the second and later copies add less. Raising k1 does the opposite. b controls length normalization, not repetition. BM25 does not ignore repeats; with k1 = 1.2 the fourth copy still adds weight.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Causal self-attention: each position may only look backward
question: Why does nanoGPT compute q, k and v for all 12 heads with one 768-to-2304 Linear instead of 36 small ones?
options: It is mathematically different and gives better accuracy
GPT-2 heads share their key matrices
It halves the parameter count
One large matrix multiply uses the GPU far better than many small ones, and gives the same result
explain: Stacking the per-head projection matrices side by side is the same linear map, so the outputs are identical. The gain is purely efficiency: one large matmul instead of many small launches. Parameter count is the same 768 x 2304 weights either way.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule
question: A friend's character-level model reaches 1.3 val loss and a colleague's BPE model 2.9. Which is better?
options: They cannot be compared: one is nats per character, the other nats per token
The character model, since 1.3 is lower
The BPE model, since 2.9 is higher
They are equal after dividing by ln 2
explain: Cross-entropy is measured per token, and the two tokenizers define different tokens over the same text. To compare you would need a per-character or per-byte measure on the same data.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: A derivative is the slope you see when you zoom in
question: A loss $L(w)$ has derivative $L'(w) = -4$ at the current weight. Which small change to $w$ lowers the loss?
options: Decrease w, because the derivative is negative
Increase w slightly: the slope is negative, so L falls as w grows
Neither: a negative derivative means you are at a minimum
Any change, because the loss is already decreasing over time
explain: A negative slope means $L$ goes down as $w$ goes up, so a small increase in $w$ lowers $L$ by about $4$ times the step. A minimum is where the derivative is zero, not negative.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
question: Training loss is going down very slowly and smoothly, and you know the gradients are correct. Which change most directly speeds things up?
options: Increase the learning rate moderately and watch for oscillation
Flip the sign of the update so you move along the gradient
Decrease the learning rate
Stop training; slow progress means a minimum was reached
explain: Smooth, slow decrease is the signature of a learning rate that is too small (like $\eta = 0.05$ here). Raise it gradually; if the loss starts to oscillate or climb you have passed the stable limit. Moving along the gradient would increase the loss.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Files, paths and permissions: finding your way around
question: You run `chmod 044 notes.txt` on a file you own, giving `----r--r--`, then `cat notes.txt` as yourself. What happens?
options: It prints the file, since everyone else can read it
It prints the file, because owners can always read their own files
chmod fails, because the owner must keep read permission
Permission denied, because only the owner bits apply to you
explain: The kernel picks one class: you own the file, so only the owner bits (`---`) count, and the group and others bits are ignored. A real run prints `cat: notes.txt: Permission denied`. You can still `chmod 644` it back, because changing the mode needs ownership, not read permission.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: File descriptors: why the order of 2>&1 matters
question: `grep -c error app.log > count.txt` prints `grep: app.log: No such file or directory` on the terminal. Why is that message not in count.txt?
options: count.txt is opened only after grep succeeds
grep prints errors through the shell, not through a file descriptor
Error messages go to fd 2, and only fd 1 was redirected
Redirection is ignored when the command fails
explain: The shell opens count.txt on fd 1 before exec, whether or not grep succeeds (so count.txt now exists, empty). grep writes its complaint to fd 2, which still points at the terminal.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Your environment and remote machines: dotfiles, ssh and tmux
question: Which approach keeps a 3-hour job running if your ssh connection to the server drops?
options: Starting it as `./job.sh &` in the ssh session
Starting it inside tmux on your laptop, then running ssh in that tmux
Adding `set -e` to job.sh
Starting it in a tmux session on the server, then detaching
explain: The tmux server on the remote machine owns the shell, so losing the connection only detaches a client. With `&` alone the job stays a job of the login shell, which forwards SIGHUP. tmux on the laptop protects only the laptop side: the ssh connection and the remote shell still die. `nohup ./job.sh &` would also survive.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Negative sampling: one word2vec update by hand
question: Why is SGNS so much cheaper per training pair than the full softmax?
options: It uses smaller vectors
It skips the input vector update
It only trains on frequent words
It touches $k + 1$ output vectors instead of all $W$
explain: The softmax normalizer needs every output vector; the negative sampling objective needs only the true context and the k samples. With k = 5 and W = 1,000,000 that is 6 dot products instead of a million.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Embeddings for IDs: categorical features, hashing and weight tying
question: A language model has a 50,000-word vocabulary and $d = 768$. How many parameters does tying the input embedding and the output softmax matrix save?
explain: Each matrix is 50,000 x 768 = 38,400,000 numbers; tying keeps one of them. (76.8 million is the size of both together.)

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory
question: A kernel is launched with only 20 thread blocks on an A100 (108 SMs), one block per SM at a time. What is the most likely problem?
options: HBM capacity is exceeded
Most SMs have no work, so the GPU is underused regardless of memory speed
The warps are too large, so threads diverge
The L2 cache is too small to hold 20 blocks
explain: Each thread block runs on one SM, so 20 blocks occupy at most 20 of 108 SMs. NVIDIA's guide recommends launching several times more blocks than SMs. This is a latency or parallelism limit, not a memory capacity issue.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token
question: A team switches a model from 32 KV heads to 8 (GQA), keeping everything else. What changes most directly?
options: KV cache per token shrinks 4x, so more or longer sequences fit and decode reads fewer cache bytes
Weights shrink by 4x
Prefill FLOPs drop 4x
Context length must be cut by 4x
explain: Only the key and value projections shrink, which are a small part of the weights. The cache stores 8 instead of 32 heads per layer, a 4x reduction in KV memory and KV traffic.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Bits, bytes and hex: how numbers are stored
question: What is `0x3c` in decimal?
explain: 3 x 16 + 12 = 60 (c is 12). In bits: 0011 1100 = 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 = 60. 36 comes from multiplying the digits, 3 x 12, and 312 from gluing the digits 3 and 12 together.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Why memory is slow and how caches hide it
question: With a 3-cycle hit time and a 240-cycle miss penalty, what is the average access time at a 5% miss rate?
options: 12 cycles
15 cycles
243 cycles
8 cycles
explain: 3 + 0.05 x 240 = 3 + 12 = 15 cycles. Note that a 5% miss rate already makes the average access 5x slower than a hit: misses dominate.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From text predictor to assistant: the three-stage recipe
question: Roughly what fraction of GPT-3's pretraining compute did the 175B InstructGPT PPO-ptx run use?
options: About 50 percent
About 16 percent
About 0.01 percent
About 1.6 percent
explain: 60 / 3,640 is about 0.0165, so about 1.6 percent. The scarce input for alignment is human data (demonstrations and comparisons), not compute.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward models: turning human comparisons into a score
question: Rewards are A = 2.0 and B = 1.0, and the human preferred B. What is the loss on this pair?
explain: The winner is B, so the gap is 1.0 - 2.0 = -1. Loss = -ln sigma(-1) = ln(1 + e) = 1.313. A wrongly ordered pair costs much more than ln 2.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward over-optimization, best-of-N and modern recipes
question: Best-of-N with N = 64 moves the output distribution how far from the base policy, by the analytic formula?
options: About 0.98 nats
About 4.16 nats
About 3.18 nats
About 64 nats
explain: log 64 - 63/64 = 4.159 - 0.984 = 3.175 nats. KL grows only logarithmically in N, which is why best-of-N is a gentle form of optimization.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
question: N = 1,000,000 and a term has df = 1,000 and tf = 3 in a document. What is its weight with raw tf, and with sublinear tf 1 + log10(tf)?
explain: idf = log10(1,000,000 / 1,000) = 3. Raw: 3 x 3 = 9. Sublinear: (1 + log10 3) x 3 = 1.477 x 3 = 4.43. Sublinear scaling halves this weight here because three occurrences count as about 1.5.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: From main.c to a running program: the four toolchain stages
question: What does `gcc -c main.c` produce?
options: An executable called a.out
Preprocessed C text on standard output
An object file main.o with unresolved references to area and printf
Assembly code in main.s
explain: -c stops after the assembler: the result is an object file. It is not runnable because the linker has not yet resolved area and printf. -E gives preprocessed text and -S gives assembly.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Integer types and conversions: where -1 > 0u
question: On 64-bit Linux, `int len = -1; size_t cap = 16;` Is `len < cap` true?
options: Yes, because -1 is less than 16
It does not compile
No, because len converts to a huge unsigned value
It is undefined behavior
explain: size_t is unsigned long here, which is wider than int, so len converts to size_t: -1 becomes 18446744073709551615, and the comparison is false. A test program printed 0 for it, and clang warned with -Wsign-compare.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Files and errors: stdio, return codes and errno
question: `char buf[8];` A file's first line is `abcdefghij` followed by a newline. What does the first `fgets(buf, sizeof buf, f)` store?
options: abcdefgh with no zero byte
The whole line, writing past the end of buf
abcdefg plus a zero byte; the next call continues with hij and the newline
Nothing: it returns NULL because the line does not fit
explain: fgets reads at most sizeof buf - 1 = 7 characters, then adds the zero byte, so buf is "abcdefg". No newline in buf tells you the line continues; the next call returns "hij" and the newline.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
question: A function creates `let s = String::from("hi");` and returns normally without doing anything else with `s`. What happens to the heap bytes?
options: They are freed when the function returns, because `s` (the owner) goes out of scope and is dropped
They leak, because there is no explicit free
They are freed later when the garbage collector runs
They stay allocated until the program exits
explain: Rule 3: when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped, and dropping a String frees its heap buffer. Rust has no tracing garbage collector, and nothing waits until exit.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Slices and why references cannot dangle
question: `let s = String::from("hello world"); let w = &s[6..11];` What does `w` hold?
options: A new heap allocation containing "world"
A pointer to byte 6 and length 11
A copy of the whole String header
A pointer to byte 6 of `s`'s buffer and length 5
explain: Slices never copy data. The range 6..11 starts at index 6 and stops before 11, so the length is 11 - 6 = 5, which is "world".

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Closures and threads: moving ownership to another thread
question: After `tx.send(msg).unwrap();` where `msg` is a String, which statement is true?
options: `msg` was moved into the channel; using it again on the sending thread is E0382
`msg` can still be read on the sending thread until the receiver calls `recv`
`send` copied the String, so both threads now have one
The String is dropped as soon as `send` returns
explain: `send` takes its argument by value. The String now belongs to the channel, and `recv` hands it to the receiver; it is dropped when the receiver's owner is. Nothing is copied, and the compiler forbids any further use on the sending side.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Matrix multiplication: composing maps and checking shapes
question: Q is $8 \times 64$ and K is $8 \times 64$. Which expression is a valid matrix product, and what is its shape?
options: Q @ K, shape 8 x 64
Q.T @ K.T, shape 64 x 64
Q @ K.T, shape 64 x 64
Q @ K.T, shape 8 x 8
explain: Inner sizes must match. $Q$ is $8\times64$ and $K^\top$ is $64\times8$, so $QK^\top$ is $8\times8$. $Q$ @ $K$ fails ($64 \ne 8$). $Q^\top K^\top$ would be $(64\times8)(64\times8)$, which also fails. This exact product returns in the last lesson, as attention scores.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues: directions a matrix only stretches
question: A quadratic loss has a Hessian with eigenvalues 8 and 0.5. Which of these learning rates is the largest that still converges along every direction?
explain: Stability needs $\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max} = 2/8 = 0.25$, so 0.24 works (factor $1 - 8 \times 0.24 = -0.92$). 4 is $2/0.5$, the limit for the flat direction only, and 1 also diverges along the sharp one. 0.125 converges but is not the largest.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: stepping downhill, and how big a step
question: A loss is quadratic with curvature 40 along its sharpest direction. Which learning rate makes plain gradient descent diverge?
explain: Stability needs $\eta < 2/40 = 0.05$. At 0.06 the factor is $1 - 40(0.06) = -1.4$, so the error grows by 40 percent per step with alternating sign. 0.025 is the one-step optimum $1/40$; 0.045 oscillates but still converges (factor -0.8).

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Validation and penalties: choosing lambda, L2 and L1
question: A teammate tunes lambda by picking the value with the lowest test error, then reports that test error as the expected performance. What is wrong?
options: Lambda was chosen to fit the test set, so the reported test error is optimistically biased; tune on a validation split instead
Nothing: the test set is the most honest measure
L2 penalties cannot be tuned, only fixed at 1
They should have picked the lambda with the lowest training error
explain: Selecting on the test set makes it part of training. Tune on validation data; report test error once at the end. Picking by training error would always choose lambda = 0, the overfit model.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Data pitfalls: leakage, distribution shift and baselines
question: A spam filter trained last year sees a new wave of spam that uses image attachments instead of text. The meaning of 'spam' has not changed. What kind of problem is this?
options: Label shift
Covariate shift: the input distribution moved
Group leakage
Overfitting to the training set
explain: The inputs (what spam looks like) changed while the rule from content to label did not: covariate shift. Label shift would be the share of spam changing while each class still looks the same.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The forward pass: layers as matrix multiplies
question: An MLP maps a 784-pixel image through one hidden layer of 100 units to 10 class scores. How many parameters (weights plus biases) does it have?
explain: Layer 1: 784 x 100 weights + 100 biases = 78,500. Layer 2: 100 x 10 weights + 10 biases = 1,010. Total 79,510. Forgetting biases gives 79,400.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backprop for a mini-batch, in matrix form
question: Why is the bias gradient the sum of $dZ$ over the batch, rather than, say, its first row?
options: The same bias vector is added to every example's row, so it affects every example's loss, and the gradients from those uses add up
Because biases are not multiplied by anything
Summing is an approximation that saves memory
Because PyTorch requires it
explain: Broadcasting copies $b$ into all $B$ rows, which is a fork: one value used in $B$ places. By the fan-out rule, the gradients from all uses add. Taking only one row would ignore how the bias affected the other examples.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
question: Under a purely cooperative OS (no timer interrupt), a process enters `while (1) {}` and never makes a system call. What happens?
options: The OS never runs again on that CPU; in practice the machine must be rebooted
The OS notices after one time slice and preempts it
The trap table automatically jumps to the scheduler after a while
The process is killed because infinite loops are privileged operations
explain: With no timer interrupt, the OS only regains control when the process makes a system call or does something illegal. An infinite loop does neither, so the OS cannot run. OSTEP notes the only recourse is to reboot. This is exactly why the timer interrupt exists.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency: race conditions and locks
question: Why does the flag-based lock fail while the test-and-set lock works?
options: Test-and-set is faster, so the window for an interrupt is smaller
The flag lock forgets to reset the flag in unlock()
The flag lock only fails on multiprocessors
Test-and-set reads the old value and writes the new one as one atomic step, so two threads cannot both see the lock as free
explain: In the flag lock, a thread can test (see 0) and then be preempted before it sets the flag, letting another thread also see 0. Test-and-set fuses test and set into a single atomic operation. Speed has nothing to do with it, and the failure happens even on one CPU with a timer interrupt.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Persistence: how a hard disk spends its time
question: A Cheetah-like disk (4 ms average seek, 2 ms average rotation, 125 MB/s transfer) reads one random 1 MB chunk. Roughly what throughput does it achieve?
options: About 125 MB/s, the peak rate
About 71 MB/s
About 0.66 MB/s, as for 4 KB reads
About 167 MB/s
explain: Transfer takes 1 MB / 125 MB/s = 8 ms, so the total is 4 + 2 + 8 = 14 ms and the rate is 1 MB / 14 ms, about 71 MB/s. Larger requests amortize the 6 ms of positioning; at 4 KB the same 6 ms dominates and gives 0.66 MB/s.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Describing data: mean, median, percentiles and outliers
question: You have 20 latency samples and want to put p99 on a dashboard. What is the main problem?
options: p99 of 20 values is decided by the largest one or two values and the interpolation rule, so it is mostly noise
p99 cannot be computed for fewer than 100 values
p99 always equals the maximum, so it adds no information
Nothing, as long as you use NumPy's default method
explain: Any rule returns a number, but with 20 samples p99 is an interpolation between the top two values, and different methods give very different answers. Only 1 in 100 values lies beyond p99, so you need many hundreds of samples before it is stable.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Random variables, expected value and variance
question: X is a die roll and Y = 7 - X (the face on the opposite side). What is Var(X + Y)?
options: Undefined, because X and Y are dependent
explain: X + Y = 7 always, a constant, so its variance is 0. Adding the variances (35/6) would be wrong because X and Y are perfectly negatively correlated, and the covariance term cancels them exactly. Linearity still gives E[X + Y] = 7.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence
question: Which statement about the KL divergence D(p || q) is true?
options: It is a true distance, so D(p || q) = D(q || p)
It can be negative when q is a better model than p
It equals the cross-entropy H(p, q) when the data are noisy
It is 0 only when q equals p, and swapping p and q can change it
explain: KL is never negative and is 0 only when the distributions match. It is not symmetric: for the example, 1.102 one way and 1.002 the other. It equals H(p, q) minus H(p), so it matches the cross-entropy only when H(p) = 0, as with one-hot labels.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Why loss falls on a straight line in log-log space
question: A run at 100M non-embedding parameters reaches the loss Kaplan's fit predicts (2.83). Using the same law with ample data, what loss should a 10B model reach?
options: About 2.38
About 1.42, half the loss for 100x the size
About 1.99
About 2.83 minus 2 x 0.45, so 1.92
explain: Two 10x steps, each multiplying loss by 0.839: $2.83 \times 0.839^2 \approx 1.99$. 2.38 is only one step (1B). Subtracting a fixed amount per step assumes a linear trend, and halving would need about 9,139x more parameters, not 100x.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Run your own scaling study: sweep, fit, extrapolate, error bars
question: Your Approach 3 fit gives $a = 0.45$ from one starting point and $a = 0.53$ from another, and both report success. What is the most likely problem?
options: The functional form is wrong, so no fit can be trusted
You need more model sizes per budget before fitting
The optimizer stopped before converging: tighten tolerances, sum rather than average the loss, and compare several starts
Noise is too high; average the two answers
explain: Two different answers on the same data mean at least one run never reached a minimum. In our example both starts settled on a = 0.508 once tolerances were tight. Averaging two unconverged fits fixes nothing, and the form itself fits these runs well.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Why you need a test collection before you can say better
question: System D is a new dense retriever evaluated on an old pooled collection. 30% of its top-10 documents were never judged. With default trec_eval settings, what happens to those documents?
options: They are skipped, and precision is computed only over judged documents
They are counted as nonrelevant, which can make D look worse than it is
They are counted as relevant, since the system found them
trec_eval refuses to score the run until they are judged
explain: trec_eval treats documents missing from the qrels like judged-nonrelevant ones. Skipping them is only done with the -J flag, which its own help text warns against using casually. If D finds relevant documents the pool missed, it gets no credit, so its score is biased downward.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow
question: Which property is what makes the bi-encoder's precomputation possible?
options: Its passage vector is a function of the passage alone
It uses cosine instead of dot product
It is a smaller model than a cross-encoder
It tokenizes the query and passage with the same vocabulary
explain: Precomputation needs the passage representation to be independent of the query. Cosine versus dot product, model size and vocabulary are all irrelevant to that; a cross-encoder can share vocabulary and still cannot precompute anything.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Why language models read subwords, not words or characters
question: A word-level model with a 50,000-word vocabulary meets the made-up product name "Zorblax" at inference. What happens?
options: It maps to the single unknown token, so the model cannot tell it apart from any other unknown word
It is split into characters automatically
It is added to the vocabulary on the fly
The model raises an error and stops
explain: A word-level vocabulary is fixed after training. Any word outside it becomes the shared `<unk>` id, losing its identity. Falling back to smaller pieces is exactly what a subword tokenizer adds; a pure word-level one has no such fallback.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Build a byte-level BPE tokenizer in Python
question: You run `train("hahaha", 256 + 2)`. h is 104 and a is 97. What is the id list after training?
explain: Merge 1: (104, 97) occurs 3 times and becomes 256 (ha), giving [256, 256, 256]. Merge 2: (256, 256) is counted twice because the pairs overlap, and becomes 257 (haha). merge scans left to right, replaces the first two and leaves the third: [257, 256].

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: WordPiece, Unigram and SentencePiece in depth
question: A LLaMA-style SentencePiece BPE model trained with byte fallback meets a character that is not in its vocabulary. What does the tokenizer output?
options: The unknown token <unk>
The most similar character in the vocabulary
The character's UTF-8 bytes, each as a byte token such as <0xE3>
Nothing: the character is dropped
explain: Byte fallback decomposes characters missing from the vocabulary into UTF-8 byte tokens, so nothing becomes unknown. The LLaMA papers describe exactly this: fall back to bytes to decompose unknown UTF-8 characters. It gives SentencePiece models the no-unknown property that byte-level BPE gets from its 256 base tokens.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Learning rate: the stability limit, warmup, decay and clipping
question: Your loss is fine for 200 steps, then spikes to NaN. Halving the learning rate fixes it, but training is now slow. Which change best addresses the cause while keeping speed?
options: Add linear warmup and global-norm gradient clipping, then return to the original peak learning rate
Increase the batch size without changing the learning rate
Switch the cosine decay to a constant learning rate
Lower the momentum to 0
explain: A late spike at an otherwise good learning rate points to occasional oversized steps. Clipping caps those rare steps without slowing ordinary ones, and warmup keeps the early, fast-changing phase stable. Halving the rate everywhere pays the cost on every step.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Batch size, gradient accumulation and tuning hyperparameters
question: You double the batch size from 256 to 512 and keep everything else. According to the tuning playbook, what most needs re-tuning?
options: Nothing: batch size only affects speed
Only the number of epochs
Only the random seed
The optimizer hyperparameters (learning rate, momentum) and the regularization strength
explain: The playbook says the best values of most hyperparameters are sensitive to the batch size, and names optimizer and regularization hyperparameters as the ones that interact most strongly with it.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Greedy search on a proximity graph, and why ef matters
question: On the toy graph, greedy search (ef = 1) returned F instead of H. Which change would most directly let it find H?
options: Start from F instead of A
Use cosine distance instead of Euclidean
Remove the edge between D and F
Raise ef so G is kept in the result list
explain: With ef = 3, G (3.0) survives in W after D is expanded, and expanding G reveals H. Changing the start node or edges is not something you control per query; ef is the query-time knob.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Dependencies and transitive trees: code you never chose
question: Your project lists 12 direct dependencies. A security advisory names a package you have never heard of. What should you do first?
options: Check the full tree (`npm ls <name>` or the lockfile) to see whether it is installed transitively
Remove all 12 direct dependencies
Delete node_modules and reinstall
Ignore it, because it is not in package.json
explain: Transitive packages are installed and run like any other. `npm ls <name>` or a search of the lockfile tells you whether, and through which path, it reached you.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Protestware: when the legitimate maintainer is the threat
question: A CI pipeline runs `npm ci` with a lockfile committed in December 2021 containing colors 1.4.0. What happens on 9 January 2022?
options: npm ci fails because a newer version exists
It installs 1.4.0, as recorded in the lockfile
It installs colors 1.4.44-liberty-2 because it is newer
It installs 1.4.1 because ^ allows minor updates
explain: `npm ci` installs exactly the lockfile. New releases only enter when someone updates the lockfile, which is the window in which review and cooldowns help.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Reproducible builds: proving a binary came from its source
question: What does a successful independent reproduction of a release binary prove?
options: That every dependency is free of vulnerabilities
That the source code contains no backdoor
That the published binary is exactly what the stated source and build instructions produce, so the build step was not tampered with
That the maintainer is trustworthy
explain: It moves trust from 'the build server was clean' to 'the source is what we think'. The source itself still needs review, and its provenance still matters.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Scanning dependencies: OSV, advisories and Dependabot
question: The scanner prints 'ok' for every package. What can you conclude?
options: The project contains no malicious or vulnerable code
All dependencies are signed
The lockfile is up to date
No advisory currently matches those exact versions in the databases queried
explain: Scanners know only what has been reported. Every malicious package in this course was 'ok' for some time after publication, which is why cooldowns and the other layers exist.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: The Gaussian loop: unbiased fits that still shrink to a point
question: A team fixes collapse in this Gaussian loop by raising M from 10 to 100 samples per generation, keeping everything else the same. What actually happens?
options: Collapse stops, because the estimator becomes accurate enough
Collapse is slowed roughly tenfold (halving time about 12 to about 137 generations) but still happens
Collapse speeds up, because more samples overfit
Nothing changes, because the estimator was already unbiased
explain: The drift of log-variance is about -1/(M-1) per generation, so a 10x larger sample makes it about 10x smaller. It never reaches zero for finite M, so sigma still tends to 0. Only fresh real data or growing sample sizes change the outcome.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Using synthetic data well: filter, diversify, anchor
question: A team fine-tunes a model on its own sampled answers to math problems, sampled at temperature 0.3, keeping all of them, for five rounds. Accuracy on their synthetic validation set rises but falls on real exam questions. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The learning rate was too high
No outside signal filters the answers and low temperature narrows the outputs, so each round reinforces the model's own errors and loses rare solution paths
Five rounds is too few for self-training to converge
Math problems cannot benefit from synthetic data
explain: This is a closed, replacing, tail-cutting loop. STaR-style filtering by correct answers, higher-diversity sampling, and keeping real data in the mix address each part. Validating on synthetic data hid the damage.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When a system call blocks: sleeping, short counts and EINTR
question: A handler for SIGCHLD is installed with SA_RESTART. Which blocked call can still fail with EINTR when SIGCHLD arrives?
options: read on a pipe
epoll_wait
waitpid
write on a socket with no timeout set
explain: signal(7) lists epoll_wait, poll and select among the calls that are never restarted, regardless of SA_RESTART. read and write on pipes and sockets, and waitpid, are restarted when the handler has SA_RESTART. Event loops therefore always check for EINTR after epoll_wait.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Shared memory between processes: MAP_SHARED, shm_open and memfd
question: Two unrelated programs, a camera daemon and a viewer, must share a 64 MiB frame buffer. The daemon should not leave a name in /dev/shm that another user could open. Which approach fits?
options: memfd_create in the daemon, then send the descriptor to the viewer over a UNIX domain socket
MAP_SHARED | MAP_ANONYMOUS in the daemon; the viewer maps the same address
shm_open with a random name, never unlinked
Write frames to a pipe; pipes are shared memory
explain: A memfd has no name in any file system; only processes holding the descriptor can map it, and memfd_create(2) lists passing it over a UNIX domain socket as one way to share it. An anonymous mapping is reachable only through fork. A shm_open name is visible in /dev/shm until unlinked. A pipe copies every byte through the kernel.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Measuring correctly: intended start times and HdrHistogram
question: Spot the bug in this load loop: `t0 = now(); send(req); resp = recv(); hist.record(now() - t0)` run back to back on 16 connections.
options: It records in milliseconds instead of microseconds
It measures from actual send time on closed-loop connections, so requests delayed while the connection was blocked are never counted
It should use the mean instead of a histogram
Nothing, 16 connections make it open-loop
explain: Each connection only sends after the previous reply, and t0 is taken at actual send. Time a request spent waiting to be sent during a stall is invisible. Fix: drive sends from a rate plan and record now() minus the intended send time.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Merging overlapping roles: union, gaps and double counting
question: In the sweep, `merged[-1][1]` is the end of the last merged block. A developer writes `merged[-1][1] = e` instead of `max(merged[-1][1], e)`. On the toy resume (generous convention), what total does the code report?
options: 132 months, the bug never triggers
180 months, it stops merging
129 months: B, nested inside A, cuts A's block short by 3 months
137 months, gaps are counted
explain: When B (ending Dec 2017) is merged into A's block, the end is overwritten from Mar 2018 to Dec 2017, losing Jan to Mar 2018. C still starts a new block, D and E extend it correctly, so the total is 31 + 98 = 129. Nested intervals are exactly the case max() exists for.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Coverage: how pass@k grows with the number of samples
question: A model has pass@1 = 0.01 on a problem. Roughly how many independent samples give a 63% chance of at least one correct answer?
options: About 10
About 63
About 100
About 1,000
explain: $1 - 0.99^{100} = 0.634$. In general, $k \approx 1/p$ samples give about $1 - 1/e = 63\%$ coverage for small $p$.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
question: A product mostly receives easy prompts that the model already solves 70% of the time. Which allocation does the paper's evidence favor?
options: Deep lookahead search against a PRM
Spend the budget sequentially (revise or keep reasoning) rather than on aggressive PRM search
Skip any verifier and return the first sample
Always use the maximum number of parallel samples
explain: On easy bins, sequential revisions did best and beam search degraded with budget. Light selection (vote or weighted best-of-N) over a revision chain is the safer choice.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading
question: During inference with a TTT model, what changes as the model reads a long prompt?
options: Nothing; all weights are frozen at inference
Only the inner weights W inside each TTT layer, which act as a per-sequence hidden state
All model parameters, via backpropagation of next-token loss on the prompt
The projections theta_K, theta_V and theta_Q, which adapt to the prompt
explain: The inner loop runs at inference, so each layer's W takes gradient steps on its self-supervised loss. The outer parameters (projections, W_0, the rest of the network) are learned in training and frozen. No next-token loss is backpropagated at inference.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
question: Which change would you expect to hurt the Titans neural memory most, according to the paper's ablation?
options: Removing the persistent memory tokens
Removing the 1D convolutions after the projections
Removing weight decay (the forget mechanism)
Replacing SiLU with GELU in the projections
explain: Table 5: without weight decay perplexity rises from 27.01 to 29.04, the largest drop, with momentum next (28.98). Persistent memory matters least (27.63). The activation swap was not tested, so the paper gives no evidence for it. SiLU multiplies x by sigmoid of x, a smooth ReLU-like curve much like GELU.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: After Titans: better objectives, optimal solvers, and replication
question: A memory keeps getting corrupted by rare tokens with huge values (say, a burst of numbers in a table). Which Miras variant targets this directly?
options: Moneta, because the l3 loss grows faster for large errors
Memora, because KL retention keeps weights on a simplex
Yaad, because the Huber loss caps how far one large error can move the memory
None; only a forget gate can help
explain: Huber is squared error for small errors and absolute error beyond delta_t, so the step size stops growing with the error and one outlier cannot drag the memory all the way to its value. An l3 loss does the opposite, weighting large errors even more, and KL retention is about how weights are kept and forgotten, not about outliers.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Sizing M, filling the depot, and the memory you pay
question: Why are full magazines only ever created as a side effect of frees, never allocated directly on the alloc path?
options: Allocating a full magazine needs M objects, which would mean M slab-layer trips, and for the magazine cache itself it would recurse forever
Full magazines are larger than empty ones
The depot lock forbids allocation
Frees are rarer than allocs
explain: Allocating empty magazines on the free path is cheap and safe. Pre-filling a magazine on the alloc path would need many objects at once, and since magazines are themselves allocated from an object cache, the first magazine allocation would need a magazine: infinite recursion. The paper notes this explicitly.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: PEAK and TaHiTI: from backlog to handover
question: A TaHiTI hunt needs 60 days of process creation events with command lines, but the domain controllers only record process creation without command lines. What is the outcome?
options: Proven: missing data means the attacker deleted it
Failed: the required data is not available, which is itself a finding
Inconclusive: run the same queries again next week
Disproven: nothing malicious was found
explain: TaHiTI says that when 'the required data may simply not be available', the hunt can be considered failed, and that 'can still lead to valuable lessons learned'. Here the lesson is a logging recommendation: enable command-line capture (event 4688 with command lines, or Sysmon) on domain controllers. Calling it disproven would claim a check that never happened.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Hunting in EDR data II: LSASS, WMI and sensors that go quiet
question: In the HSE timeline, antivirus detected Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz on 31 March in monitor mode. Which recurring hunt would most directly have surfaced it?
options: Stacking the DNS names every workstation resolves
A weekly review of all security-control detections, grouped by threat name and device, including ones not blocked
Baselining VPN logins
Searching for the ransomware's file hash
explain: The evidence was a detection already recorded by a security control. Grouping all such detections by tool name and device, and treating 'not blocked' or 'remediated' as still needing a look, puts two well-known attack tools on one workstation at the top of the list. The ransomware hash did not exist on that machine until 14 May.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: From hunt to detection: the FireEye countermeasures
question: A hunt for Office applications starting shells found one real intrusion and three benign matches over four weeks. When it becomes a detection, what should those four events become?
options: Allowlist entries for all four
A threat intelligence report
Test cases: the intrusion as must-match, the three benign matches as must-not-match
Nothing; they are history
explain: The hunt has produced labelled examples, which is precisely what a detection's unit tests need. The real event proves the rule still fires after future changes; the benign ones measure and guard against false positives. Allowlisting the true positive would hide the very thing the rule exists to catch.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Strategic, operational, tactical and technical intelligence
question: Which product is *operational* intelligence in the MWR and NCSC sense that FIRST summarises?
options: A warning to the CISO that a group hitting two sector peers this week uses the same VPN model you run
A list of 2,000 malicious domains for the web proxy
A ten-year forecast of state-sponsored espionage trends for the board
A YARA rule for a malware family
explain: Operational intelligence is specific to the organisation and warns defenders of an impending attack. The domain list and the YARA rule are technical (or tactical, depending on convention), and the ten-year forecast is strategic.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: The Diamond Model: one event, four corners
question: Your endpoint detection tool found malware on one laptop and you have the C2 domain from reversing it. Which pivot is most likely to find other compromised machines in your own network?
options: Search DNS and proxy logs for other hosts that resolved or contacted the C2 domain and its IPs
Look up the adversary's motive
Check the malware's capacity against CVE lists
Wait for the attacker's next phishing email
explain: That is the infrastructure-to-victim pivot (pivot 4 in the paper's example): hosts talking to the same C2 infrastructure are candidate victims. It uses data you already hold, which is why victim-centred work starts there.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Analytic tradecraft: bias and competing hypotheses
question: Why did Kaspersky treat the identical Rich header with suspicion rather than as proof?
options: The header's contents contradicted the binary it was attached to, and a 100% match with a famous group seemed too convenient
Rich headers are encrypted and cannot be read
Lazarus never uses Windows
TLP:RED forbade attribution
explain: The header described a Visual Studio 6 build while the code could only come from Visual Studio 2010's runtime, so it had been copied in. Combined with other inconsistencies, the 'perfect' match pointed to a false flag.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: What a threat model is: four questions before the code
question: A product manager asks: 'Is our app secure?' What is the threat modeler's best first reply?
options: Secure against whom, protecting what, and for how long?
Yes, because we use HTTPS and hashed passwords
No system is secure, so the question is meaningless
Run a vulnerability scanner and report the score
explain: Security is relative to an adversary and an asset. Listing controls (HTTPS) answers question 3 before questions 1 and 2. A scanner finds some implementation bugs but says nothing about design threats.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: STRIDE per element: from a diagram to a threat list
question: Why does STRIDE per element NOT list spoofing for a data store?
options: Data stores are always encrypted
Spoofing applies to things that have an identity to fake, like users and processes; a store's threats are its data being changed, read, or made unavailable
Data stores sit inside the trust boundary
Spoofing is the same as tampering
explain: The table records where threats cluster in practice. Stores are not always encrypted or internal, and spoofing differs from tampering: one fakes an identity, the other changes data.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Design principles II: least privilege, two keys and shared parts
question: A payment system lets one clerk both create a new supplier and approve payments to it. Which principle is missing?
options: Least common mechanism
Separation of privilege: creating a payee and approving payment should need two different people
Fail-safe defaults
Work factor
explain: With both powers in one pair of hands, a single dishonest or deceived person can pay themselves. Two keys held by different people means no single breach of trust is enough.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Why memory is becoming a hierarchy of tiers
question: A service has 200 GB allocated, of which 40 GB is touched every few seconds and the rest is idle for minutes. Which configuration best fits tiered memory?
options: 64 GB DRAM and 160 GB CXL, with the OS demoting idle pages to CXL
160 GB DRAM and 40 GB CXL, so hot pages are guaranteed to fit
200 GB of CXL only, since CXL is cheaper per GB
64 GB DRAM and 160 GB of SSD swap, since swap is cheapest
explain: The hot 40 GB fits in 64 GB of DRAM with headroom, and idle pages go to cheaper CXL where they remain directly addressable. All-CXL puts hot data 2x farther away, and swap-only makes every access to a cold page a fault plus an SSD read.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: The SSD tier, zswap, and running tiering in production
question: Why does TPP not use CXL memory as a fast swap device instead of a NUMA node?
options: Swap cannot be placed on byte-addressable memory
CXL devices do not support writes
Swap semantics turn every access into a major fault and a full-page copy, losing CXL's direct cache-line loads
The kernel cannot migrate pages to CXL
explain: The value of CXL is that warm pages can be read in place with a load at roughly 2x DRAM latency. Treating it as swap would add a fault and a 4 KiB copy to every access to a swapped page.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: What TLS promises, and what it does not
question: A user connects over HTTPS to a phishing site, `paypa1-login.example`, which has a valid certificate for that exact name. Which TLS promise failed?
options: None: TLS authenticated paypa1-login.example correctly; deciding it is the wrong site is outside TLS
Authentication, because the certificate is fake
Confidentiality, because the attacker can read the traffic
Integrity, because the page content was changed
explain: TLS binds the connection to the name the client asked for. The certificate is genuine for that name. Look-alike domains are a human and policy problem (and a reason CT monitoring exists), not a protocol failure.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: TLS 1.2, RSA key exchange and forward secrecy
question: A bank's server used TLS 1.2 with `TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256` for five years. Its private key leaks today. What can an attacker who recorded traffic for those five years do?
options: Decrypt the recorded sessions, because each premaster secret was encrypted to that key
Nothing, because AES-GCM is still secure
Only impersonate the bank from now on
Decrypt only sessions from the last 24 hours
explain: TLS_RSA_ suites use RSA key exchange: the premaster secret of every session was RSA-encrypted to the leaked key. AES-GCM being strong does not help when the key that protects its keys is gone.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Hostname checks and the code that turns verification off
question: A developer gets `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED` talking to `https://billing.internal`, whose certificate comes from the company's private CA. What is the right fix?
options: Set verify=False for that one call
Set check_hostname=False but keep CERT_REQUIRED
Load the company root CA into the client's trust settings (for example cafile=...) and keep both checks on
Switch to plain HTTP inside the network
explain: The error is correct: the client does not know the private CA. Teaching it that CA keeps full authentication. Disabling either check lets any machine on the path impersonate billing.internal.
